rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: The length of perpendicular drawn from the point (3, 4, 2) on the line \(\frac{x}{0} = \frac{y}{0} = \frac{z}{1}\) is
rows.solution: The line \(\frac{x}{0} = \frac{y}{0} = \frac{z}{1}\) passes through the origin with direction ratios \(<0, 0, 1>\), so it is the z-axis. The foot of the perpendicular from \((3, 4, 2)\) to the z-axis is \((0, 0, 2)\), so the required length is \(\sqrt{(3-0)^2 + (4-0)^2 + (2-2)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5\). Equivalently, the distance of a point from the z-axis is \(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\). So the length of the perpendicular is 5.

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.solution: For every \(x\) in its domain \([-1, 1]\), \(\sin^{-1} x\) lies in the principal value branch \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), and both endpoints ARE attained (at \(x = -1\) and \(x = 1\)), so the inequalities are non-strict. Adding \(\pi\) throughout \(-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \sin^{-1} x \le \frac{\pi}{2}\) gives \(-\frac{\pi}{2} + \pi \le y \le \frac{\pi}{2} + \pi\), that is \(\frac{\pi}{2} \le y \le \frac{3\pi}{2}\).

rows.stem: If \(A = [a_{ij}]_{3 \times 3}\) is a scalar matrix then which of the following must be true ?

options.label: A
options.text: A must be a symmetric matrix.

options.label: B
options.text: A must be a skew-symmetric matrix.

options.label: C
options.text: A must be an identity matrix.

options.label: D
options.text: A must be a null matrix.

rows.solution: A scalar matrix is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are all equal, so \(A = kI\) for some scalar \(k\). Then \(A' = (kI)' = kI' = kI = A\), so A is always symmetric. None of the other three is forced: A is skew-symmetric only in the special case \(k = 0\), it is the identity matrix only if \(k = 1\), and it is the null matrix only if \(k = 0\). So the only property that must be true is that A is a symmetric matrix.

rows.stem: If A and B are symmetric matrics of same order, then \((AB - BA)\) is a
rows.solution: Since A and B are symmetric, \(A' = A\) and \(B' = B\). Using \((PQ)' = Q'P'\), \((AB - BA)' = (AB)' - (BA)' = B'A' - A'B' = BA - AB = -(AB - BA)\). A matrix whose transpose is its own negative is skew-symmetric, so \(AB - BA\) is a skew symmetric matrix. (It need not be the zero matrix: that happens only when A and B commute, and it can never be the identity matrix, since every diagonal entry of a skew-symmetric matrix is zero.)

rows.subtopic: Absolute Maximum and Minimum on a Closed Interval
rows.stem: The least value of \(f(x) = e^{-x}\) in [0, 3] is
rows.solution: \(f(x) = e^{-x}\) has \(f'(x) = -e^{-x}\), which is negative for every \(x\), so \(f\) is strictly decreasing on \([0, 3]\) and has no interior critical point. A decreasing function takes its least value at the right-hand endpoint, so the least value is \(f(3) = e^{-3}\). (The negative choices can be ruled out at once, since \(e^{-x} > 0\) for every real \(x\), and the value 1 is \(f(0)\), the greatest value on this interval, not the least.)

rows.subtopic: Order and Degree of a Differential Equation
rows.stem: The order and degree of the differential equation : \(\frac{d}{dx}(y')^3 + (y')^3 = 1\) respectively are where \(y' = \frac{dy}{dx}\)
rows.solution: First carry out the differentiation: \(\frac{d}{dx}(y')^3 = 3(y')^2 y''\), so the equation reads \(3(y')^2 y'' + (y')^3 = 1\). The highest-order derivative appearing is \(y'' = \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), so the order is 2. The equation is a polynomial in the derivatives, and the highest-order derivative \(y''\) occurs to the first power, so the degree is 1. Hence the order and degree are 2, 1. (The exponent 3 belongs to \(y'\), which is not the highest-order derivative, so it does not set the degree.)

Use \(1 + \cos 2x = 2\cos^2 x\), so \(\sqrt{\frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\cos^2 x}{2}} = \left|\cos x\right|\), which equals \(\cos x\) because \(\cos x > 0\) on \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Now write \(\cos x = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), giving \(\sin^{-1}\left(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\right)\). For \(0 < x < \frac{\pi}{2}\) the angle \(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\) itself lies in \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), which is inside the principal branch \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) of \(\sin^{-1}\), so the expression simplifies to \(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\).

Take the two inverse functions in turn. \(\sin^{-1}(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{2}\), the endpoint of the principal branch \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\); and \(\tan^{-1}\left(-\sqrt{3}\right) = -\frac{\pi}{3}\), since \(\tan\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\sqrt{3}\) and \(-\frac{\pi}{3}\) lies in \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Hence the expression is \(\cos\left[-\frac{\pi}{2} - \left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right] = \cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \cos\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

rows.stem: Using vectors, find the area of \(\Delta ABC\) with vertices A(1, 2, 3), B(2, -1, 4) and C(4, 5, -1).
rows.solution: Take the two sides meeting at A as vectors: \(\vec{AB} = (2-1)\hat{i} + (-1-2)\hat{j} + (4-3)\hat{k} = \hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(\vec{AC} = (4-1)\hat{i} + (5-2)\hat{j} + (-1-3)\hat{k} = 3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}\). Then \(\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & 3 & -4 \end{vmatrix} = (12 - 3)\hat{i} - (-4 - 3)\hat{j} + (3 + 9)\hat{k} = 9\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}\). The area of the triangle is half the magnitude of this cross product: \(\frac{1}{2}\left|\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}\right| = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{81 + 49 + 144} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{274}\) square units.

Integrate by parts with \(\log\left(1 + x^2\right)\) as the first function and 1 as the second: \(\int_{0}^{1} \log\left(1 + x^2\right)dx = \left[x\log\left(1 + x^2\right)\right]_{0}^{1} - \int_{0}^{1} \frac{2x}{1 + x^2} \cdot x\,dx = \log 2 - 2\int_{0}^{1} \frac{x^2}{1 + x^2}\,dx\). Now write \(\frac{x^2}{1 + x^2} = \frac{\left(1 + x^2\right) - 1}{1 + x^2} = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\), so \(\int_{0}^{1} \frac{x^2}{1 + x^2}\,dx = \left[x - \tan^{-1} x\right]_{0}^{1} = 1 - \frac{\pi}{4}\). Therefore the value of the integral is \(\log 2 - 2\left(1 - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \log 2 - 2 + \frac{\pi}{2}\).

rows.stem:
Find the general solution of the differential equation
\((y^2 - x^2)dx = 2xy \, dy\)
rows.solution: Both sides are homogeneous of degree 2, so write the equation as \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y^2 - x^2}{2xy} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{y}{x} - \frac{x}{y}\right]\). Put \(y = vx\), so that \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\). The equation becomes \(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{1}{2}\left[v - \frac{1}{v}\right]\), so \(x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{v^2 - 1}{2v} - v = -\frac{1 + v^2}{2v}\). Separating the variables, \(\frac{2v\,dv}{1 + v^2} = -\frac{dx}{x}\), and integrating both sides gives \(\log\left(1 + v^2\right) = -\log|x| + \log C\), that is \(\log\left(\left(1 + v^2\right)|x|\right) = \log C\), so \(\left(1 + v^2\right)x = C\). Restoring \(v = \frac{y}{x}\), \(\left(1 + \frac{y^2}{x^2}\right)x = C\), which simplifies to the general solution \(x^2 + y^2 = Cx\).

rows.stem:
Find the particular solution of the differential equation
\((1 + e^{2x})dy + (1 + y^2)e^x\,dx = 0\), given that \(y(1) = 0\).
rows.solution: [CBSE marking scheme: the first line of the printed solution writes \(\frac{dy}{1 + y^2} = \frac{e^x}{1 + e^{2x}}dx\), dropping the minus sign that rearranging \(\left(1 + e^{2x}\right)dy + \left(1 + y^2\right)e^x dx = 0\) produces. The scheme restores it on the very next line and its final answer is correct; only that one printed line is out.] Rearranging the equation, \(\left(1 + e^{2x}\right)dy = -\left(1 + y^2\right)e^x dx\), so \(\frac{dy}{1 + y^2} = -\frac{e^x}{1 + e^{2x}}dx\). Integrating, \(\int\frac{dy}{1 + y^2} = -\int\frac{e^x}{1 + e^{2x}}dx\). For the right side substitute \(e^x = t\), so \(e^x dx = dt\) and \(1 + e^{2x} = 1 + t^2\), giving \(-\int\frac{dt}{1 + t^2} = -\tan^{-1} t = -\tan^{-1}\left(e^x\right)\). Hence \(\tan^{-1} y + \tan^{-1}\left(e^x\right) = C\). Applying \(y(1) = 0\): \(\tan^{-1} 0 + \tan^{-1}(e) = C\), so \(C = \tan^{-1}(e)\). The required particular solution is \(\tan^{-1} y + \tan^{-1}\left(e^x\right) = \tan^{-1}(e)\).

rows.stem: Show that line AB passing through points A(0, 4, 1), B(2, 3, -1) and the line CD passing through points C(4, 5, 0), D(2, 6, 2) are parallel. Also, find distance between them.
rows.solution: The direction ratios of AB are \(\vec{AB} = <2 - 0,\; 3 - 4,\; -1 - 1> = <2, -1, -2>\), and those of CD are \(\vec{CD} = <2 - 4,\; 6 - 5,\; 2 - 0> = <-2, 1, 2>\). Since \(<-2, 1, 2> = -1 \cdot <2, -1, -2>\), the two direction vectors are proportional, so the lines AB and CD are parallel. In vector form they are \(\vec{r} = 4\hat{j} + \hat{k} + \lambda\left(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\right)\) and \(\vec{r} = 4\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + \mu\left(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\right)\), so \(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1} = 4\hat{i} + \hat{j} - \hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\). Then \(\left(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1}\right) \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2 \end{vmatrix} = (-2 - 1)\hat{i} - (-8 + 2)\hat{j} + (-4 - 2)\hat{k} = -3\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}\). The distance between the parallel lines is \(\frac{\left|\left(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1}\right) \times \vec{b}\right|}{\left|\vec{b}\right|} = \frac{\sqrt{9 + 36 + 36}}{\sqrt{4 + 1 + 4}} = \frac{9}{3} = 3\) units.

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Functions in Parametric Form
rows.stem: If \(x = a(\sin t - t \cos t)\) and \(y = b(\cos t + t \sin t)\), then find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\).
rows.solution: Differentiate each coordinate with respect to \(t\), using the product rule on the second term each time. \(\frac{dx}{dt} = a\left(\cos t - \left[\cos t - t\sin t\right]\right) = at\sin t\), and \(\frac{dy}{dt} = b\left(-\sin t + \left[\sin t + t\cos t\right]\right) = bt\cos t\). Hence \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{bt\cos t}{at\sin t} = \frac{b}{a}\cot t\). For the second derivative, differentiate this with respect to \(t\) and multiply by \(\frac{dt}{dx}\): \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -\frac{b}{a}\operatorname{cosec}^2 t \cdot \frac{dt}{dx}\). Since \(\frac{dx}{dt} = at\sin t\), we have \(\frac{dt}{dx} = \frac{1}{at\sin t}\), so \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -\frac{b}{a}\operatorname{cosec}^2 t \cdot \frac{1}{at\sin t} = -\frac{b\operatorname{cosec}^3 t}{a^2 t}\).
